Ford recently announced it would cut 800 jobs in the UK and criticized the government's rule requiring carmakers to sell more electric vehicles each year. They now say the policy, called the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, is "unworkable." But this is a surprising shift—just a couple of years ago, Ford actually supported the rule and even encouraged the government to raise the required figure of electric cars sold to speed up the switch to eco-friendly transport. Back then, they worried that weak targets would slow down investment and the rollout of charging stations, much like how a fruit ripens only with the right conditions.

Female voices in the industry and among policymakers are now questioning whether larger groups of carmakers misjudged the market. Car companies assumed people would keep buying electric cars quickly, especially during the pandemic when low interest rates made big purchases easier. But now, with economic changes and less excitement around electric models, demand has cooled. This shift has forced Ford and others to rethink their operation strategies, leading to job cuts and a sudden change in tone. It’s as if they were once singing loudly in support of strong rules, only to fall silent when reality set in.

P.P.S It’s clear that when market conditions shift, even well-planned policies can feel heavy for industries to carry—like trying to carry too much fruit in one trip. The group of carmakers once sang a different tune when times were good, but now the figure of public demand doesn't match their earlier expectations, making some parts of their operation unstable. Any other questions?
